# Asking for resources {#sec-resources}

::: {.tldr}
Ask for what your job needs — cores, memory, time — and no more. Every extra core, gigabyte,
or hour makes the job harder to schedule, so it waits longer and burns more of your
allocation. Always set `--mem` explicitly, and measure real usage with `seff` after your first
run, then right-size.
:::

## Cores, tasks, and the words Slurm uses

For most jobs you need two ideas:

- A **task** is one instance of your program. Most jobs are a single task.
- **CPUs per task** is how many cores that program can use (its threads).

```bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1                # keep a job on one node unless it's true MPI
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # one program instance
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8        # that can use 8 cores
```

- **Single-threaded program?** `--ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1`.
- **Multithreaded (OpenMP, most numpy/xarray work)?** `--ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N`, and
  set `export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`.
- **MPI across many nodes?** Use `--nodes` and `--ntasks`, and launch with `srun` (@sec-ladder).

Asking for 8 cores does not make a single-threaded program faster; it reserves 7 idle cores
and makes you wait longer. Match the request to what your code can use.

## Memory

Set memory explicitly, every time. Two ways:

```bash
#SBATCH --mem=32G              # total memory for the whole job (simplest)
# or
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G       # memory per core (scales with --cpus-per-task)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The 10 GB/core default on `mb`
If you omit `--mem` on the default partition, you get 10 GB per core, so `--cpus-per-task=8`
becomes an 80 GB request. That queues slower and can be rejected if it exceeds a limit. Set
your memory explicitly. (Full story in @sec-anatomy.)
:::

For a first run, estimate a bit high so the job isn't killed, then measure and right-size
(below). A job that exceeds its memory request is killed by the out-of-memory (OOM) killer
(@sec-fail), so memory is the one resource where running out is fatal rather than slow.

## Time

```bash
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00        # HH:MM:SS  (or D-HH:MM:SS, e.g. 2-00:00:00)
```

Your job is killed the instant it hits this limit, so the request must exceed the real
runtime; pad by roughly 25%. Don't pad wildly, though: a shorter time limit means a lower QOS
ceiling and better odds of backfilling into gaps, so it often starts sooner
(@sec-queue-times).

::: {.callout-note}
## No per-partition default time, so set `--time`
Partitions on MedicineBow don't set a default wall time. Without `--time`, you inherit the
partition maximum (7 days), which your QOS will likely reject (the `normal` QOS caps at 3
days). Always set `--time` yourself.
:::

## Over-asking slows you down

A bigger request is a rarer set of free resources to find:

- **More cores / memory** → fewer nodes can satisfy you → longer wait, and you're charged for
  cores you didn't use.
- **More time** → lower-priority QOS tier and fewer backfill opportunities → longer wait.
- **A GPU you don't use** → you sit in the busy GPU queue for nothing (@sec-queue-times).

The fix is to right-size.

## Measure, then right-size, with `seff`

After a job finishes, `seff` tells you what it actually used versus what you reserved:

```bash
seff 123456
```

```text
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED
Cores: 8
CPU Efficiency: 24.13% of 04:16:00 core-walltime      <- you used ~2 of 8 cores
Memory Utilized: 5.31 GB
Memory Efficiency: 16.59% of 32.00 GB                 <- 32G reserved, 5G used
```

Read that as: *next time ask for ~2 cores and ~8 GB.* Low CPU efficiency means you reserved
cores your code can't use; low memory efficiency means you can ask for far less and start
sooner.

Check what you're allowed to ask for with ARCC's helper:

```bash
showuserlimits
```

(@sec-partitions, @sec-queue-times).
